summary: Two new records for the largest known prime were set via the Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search (GIMPS): on August 23 UCLA systems engineer Edson Smith confirmed the primality of 2^43,112,609−1, a 12,978,189‑digit Mersenne prime that qualifies GIMPS for the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s $100,000 prize (Smith said the discovery was "quite unexpected"), and on September 6 German electrical engineer Hans‑Michael Elvenich of Lanxess found 2^37,156,667−1, an 11,185,272‑digit prime that does not qualify for the prize (Elvenich called it "finally a great success" after four years in GIMPS). Both numbers were verified over several weeks by multiple GIMPS verification‑team members using different software and 16‑core systems and were announced by GIMPS on September 16; under GIMPS’ prize agreement $50,000 will go to the UCLA Department of Mathematics, $25,000 to charity, $20,000 will be split among previous discoverers of Mersenne primes, and GIMPS will keep the remainder. The article notes Mersenne primes (one less than a power of two) are rare with 46 known, GIMPS—founded by George Woltman in 1996—has found 12 of them, smaller primes are often used in cryptography while these recently discovered primes are too large to have much practical value, and the GIMPS community is already looking toward finding a 100 million‑digit prime that would qualify for a $150,000 EFF prize.
